proves: each of the five ways a mask can be written keeps a different part of the same box, and the unmasked control keeps all of it. Masking was unimplemented until this fixture's commit: Effects.mask was read in two places, both asking whether the node needed an isolation layer, and nothing applied it.
checkable: 392x56, six 56x40 cells at y=8..47, each a box filled 40,80,220 on white, at x=8, 72, 136, 200, 264 and 328. Read the middle row, y=28, at the cell's own x+0, +16, +48. Cell 0 (control) is 40,80,220 at all three. Cell 1 (circle) is white at +0 and +48 and blue at +16. Cell 2 (ellipse) is blue at +0, +16 and +48. Cell 3 (path) is white at +0 and +48 and blue at +16. Cell 4 (gradient) ramps along the row: 42,81,220 at +0, 103,131,230 at +16, 226,232,250 at +48. Cell 5 (image) is blue at +0 and +16 and white at +48.
checkable_above_and_below: the middle row alone says which columns a mask keeps and nothing about which rows, and a mask applied as a horizontal band would pass it - `borders-square` failed exactly that way. Read y=12 and y=44 as well, at the same three offsets. At both rows the circle is white at +0 and +48; the ellipse is white at +0 and +48 too, which is the point: the two arms agree everywhere except the middle row, and that is where they are read apart. The path is white at all three at y=12, the apex being narrower than the offsets, and blue at +16 and +48 at y=44 where the base is wide. The control is 40,80,220 at all three offsets on all three rows, and any masked cell matching it row for row is an ignored mask.
expected: a mask keeps the box where the mask has alpha and clears it where it does not. Circle takes the largest circle that fits, so in a 56x40 cell its radius is 20 and it reaches x+8..x+48. Ellipse fills the box, so it reaches both ends of the middle row. The triangle's apex is at the top middle, so the middle row is narrower than the base. The gradient is opaque at the left and clear at the right. The image is an 8x8 whose left half is opaque.
why_the_cells_are_not_square: in a square box the largest circle that fits and the ellipse that fills it are the same shape, and a fixture of squares would pass with those two arms swapped. 56x40 separates them: the only row where they disagree is the one the checkable reads.
why_a_control_cell: property_effect.rs already proves each arm changes the picture. What a control pair cannot say is which pixels changed, and that is the distinction the border defect turned on - a fix that moved something passed a middle-row sample while the bottom edge was still a diagonal. Cell 0 is what every other cell is read against.
the_image_asset: assets/mask-half.png, beside the scene source rather than in this directory: it is source for the scene, not an artefact of it. A mask image is read for its alpha, and every one of strip.png's thirty-two pixels is opaque - a cell built on that asset would keep the whole box however well masking works, which is the same class of mistake as a dither probe on a ramp too steep to band.
status: measured from the committed image. Masking landed in the commit that added this fixture, so these numbers are the working behaviour and the fixture guards it. Any cell reading 40,80,220 across its whole middle row again is the regression it exists to catch - that is what an ignored mask looks like.
